- Copy their files to the company storage first, then open one of them to check that the copy works (right)
- Wipe it as they asked, since that is the quickest way to a clean laptop — if chosen: The month-end file would be gone, and it goes out Friday.
- Remove the add-in right away, since it is the likeliest cause — if chosen: Removing it is already a change to their laptop, and their files are not safe yet.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: The records name a change they did not mention, the add-in. They also show no backup, and a wipe would erase the file they need on Friday. Find the change, then copy the files, then fix.
The working:
- Read their words.: Slow since last week, Excel crashes on one file, they want a wipe, and they say nothing changed.
- Guess a change, and check it against the records.: First guess: a Windows update. The records show none in 30 days, so that guess is out.
- Look at what else changed.: A PDF add-in went on Monday of last week. That fits “since last week”, so it is the lead.
- Before you touch anything, protect their files.: A wipe would erase the month-end file and no backup exists. Copy their files, then open one from the copy.
- Then have them show you.: They open the month-end file and Excel crashes while you watch. Now you can take the add-in out and see whether the crash is gone.

- The fault is the server that holds the folder. — if chosen: Tom opened the price list from the same server a moment ago.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: Dana’s laptop reached a web page, so the Wi-Fi was ruled out. Tom opened the file, so the server and the file were ruled out. The same failure on Tom’s computer put the fault with Dana’s account. Three cheap tests, each cutting the list, instead of a fix on whatever was nearest.
The working:
- Write down every cause that fits, before testing any.: Dana’s laptop and its connection; Dana’s account and the folder it may not be allowed into; the server that holds the shared drive; the file itself.
- Name your favorite, and keep it as the first thing to test, not the answer.: The Wi-Fi: three people on that floor complained about it last week.
- Run the cheapest test of the favorite.: Dana opens a web page on their laptop. It opens. The laptop reaches the internet, so the Wi-Fi is working and is not the cause. One cause is gone.
- Cut what is left with another person.: Tom, next to Dana, opens the price list on Tom’s computer. It opens. The server and the file are fine. Left: Dana’s laptop, or Dana’s account.
- Cut again: the person or the computer?: Dana signs in on Tom’s computer. It fails there too. The fault goes with Dana, not their laptop.
- Look at the one cause left.: Dana joined the sales team last week and the folder’s list of people does not have them yet. Have the folder’s owner add them.

#### Question in the draw: l8-w-lockout

An email: "Rui Santos, Sales", Email · 11:40 AM.

> Subject: **Locked out AGAIN**
>
> This is the THIRD time this week my laptop has locked me out.
> Nobody there knows what they are doing.
> I have a client call at 2 and I cannot even sign in.

Rui has three tickets this week for the same lockout.

A plain table, "This desk’s rule":

> Rule  (the column heads)
> The same fault on three tickets in a week is raised as a problem.

**What is your first reply to Rui?**
(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)
- Three lockouts in a week, with a client call at 2, is a real problem and I am sorry. I need to check it is you with the desk’s usual questions; then I unlock you, and I will write you by 1:00 either way. (right)
- I am sorry about the trouble, Rui, but the earlier tickets were closed because nobody answered our follow-up. After the desk’s questions I unlock you, and I will write you by 1:00 either way. — if chosen: Rui reads it as “it is your fault”. They write back angrier and the call is still at 2.
- I am sorry about the three lockouts, Rui. After the desk’s questions I unlock you now, and I guarantee it will never lock you out again. I will write you by 1:00 either way. — if chosen: You do not know the cause yet. If it locks them out on Friday, they remember the guarantee.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: They are upset because their work is stopped. The reply says that you heard it (three times, a call at 2), says you are sorry for the trouble, does the desk’s check, and gives your next steps and a time. It does not argue about the earlier tickets and it does not promise a result you do not control.
The working:
- Do not defend the desk.: They are right that it has happened three times. Explaining why the earlier tickets were closed would be arguing, and it does not get them to the call. Say that you heard them.
- Confirm it is them.: They are upset and in a hurry, which is how someone pretending to be them would sound too. Before any unlock, the desk’s own check comes first: its usual questions, answered correctly.
- Say what happens next, and when.: They need to know that someone has it and when they will hear. Your steps and a time you will report back are in your hands. A result such as “it will never lock you out again” is not.
- Follow up at the time you said.: At 1:00 you write to them, even if you have no answer yet. A user who hears nothing feels ignored a second time. The desk’s rule raises the same fault on three tickets in a week as a problem, and Rui has three, so you hand the pattern on as a problem.

#### Question in the draw: l27-w-change

A chat, with its history: "Mr. Okafor, Finance", Chat with the help desk.

> (Mr. Okafor, Finance, at the left) Please update the firmware on the accounting server tonight. It only takes ten minutes, and payroll runs Monday morning. The server is working normally.

A plain table, "From the desk’s change rules":

> Rule  (the column heads)
> A routine change with a written, pre-approved procedure is a standard change.
> An emergency change is only for an outage or an attack that is happening now.
> Every other change to a server needs a request form, a rollback plan, a backup, a test, and the change board’s approval.
> Server changes happen in the maintenance window, Saturday 10 p.m. to 2 a.m.
> No written procedure covers firmware updates.

**Which type of change is this?**
(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)
- A normal change: not routine, and nothing is down (right)
- An emergency change, because Mr. Okafor wants it done tonight — if chosen: Wanting it tonight does not make it an emergency. The rule is an outage or an attack happening now, and neither is on the ticket.
- A standard change, because it only takes ten minutes — if chosen: Standard means a routine change with a pre-approved written procedure. How long it takes does not decide the type.
- Not a change, because the server keeps working — if chosen: A firmware update can stop the server, which is why it is a change. What matters is the risk to people’s work.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: The type comes from the desk’s rule, not from the wish for tonight. Nothing was down, so it is a normal change: a request form, rollback and backup plans, a test, board approval, the maintenance window, a peer review and the users’ acceptance.
The working:
- Name the favorite type and check it against the desk’s own rule.: The first guess is emergency, because Mr. Okafor said “tonight”. The rule needs one answer: is there an outage or an attack now? No. Emergency is ruled out.
- Write the request form.: Purpose: current firmware, fixes a fault the maker listed. Scope: the accounting server only. Type: normal. Affected systems: accounting and payroll. Risk: a failed update could stop payroll, so the risk level is high.
- Get the four things ready before the board sees it.: Rollback plan: keep the old firmware file and the steps to put it back. Backup plan: a full backup and a copy of the settings first. Sandbox testing: run the update on the spare server. Responsible staff: you do the work; the senior technician answers for it.
- Pick the time.: Not tonight. The change board must approve, and servers change only in the maintenance window: the coming Saturday. The year-end change freeze, if one were running, would block it altogether.
- After approval, do the work, get it checked, and get the users to accept it.: Implement it Saturday. A second technician reviews it (peer review). On Monday, Mr. Okafor confirms payroll runs (end-user acceptance). Write the note: the approval, the backup and the check. Then close the ticket.

- The purpose: why the change is wanted — if chosen: The purpose gives the reason. This text lists what is included.
- The type: standard, normal or emergency — if chosen: The type names the kind of change. This text names the systems it covers.
- The date and time: when the change will happen — if chosen: The date and time say when. This text says what.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: The scope of a change is what it covers and what it does not.

#### Question in the draw: l27-k-change

A chat, with its history: "Chidi, Network", Chat with the help desk.

> (Chidi, Network, at the left) I changed the branch firewall rules (the filter between networks) yesterday. Today the branch cannot reach the main office, and nobody wrote down any steps for undoing what I did.

**Which part of change management was missing?**
(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)
- A rollback plan, the exact steps to undo the change (right)
- End-user acceptance, where users confirm that it works — if chosen: Acceptance comes after the work and confirms it. It does not give the way back.
- A change freeze, a time when changes are not allowed at all — if chosen: A freeze blocks changes during a period. It is not a plan for undoing one.
- A risk analysis, which rates how likely harm is — if chosen: A risk analysis rates the danger before the change. It does not say how to undo it.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: Steps for undoing a change that goes wrong are the rollback plan, one of the four things that must be ready before approval.

#### Question in the draw: l27-r-change-1

A chat, with its history: "Carmen, Network", Chat with the help desk.

**What is that agreed time called?**
(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)
- A maintenance window agreed with the board (right)
- A change freeze, which blocks changes for a period — if chosen: A change freeze is a time when changes are not allowed.
- End-user acceptance, a check after the work — if chosen: End-user acceptance is the users confirming the finished change works for them.
- Sandbox testing, a trial run on a copy — if chosen: Sandbox testing is a trial in a safe copy, not a time slot for the live change.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: A time agreed for making changes, usually when few people work, is a maintenance window.

#### Question in the draw: l27-r-change-2

(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)

- A rollback plan: the written steps that undo a change — if chosen: A rollback plan is written steps for going back. A trial run on a copy is something else.
- A backup plan: a copy of the data taken beforehand — if chosen: A backup plan copies the data. Here, the update itself is being tried on a copy.
- A peer review: a second technician checks the finished work — if chosen: A peer review checks finished work. Here the update has not been applied to anything live.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: Trying a change in a safe copy first is sandbox testing.

#### Question in the draw: l27-r-change-3

- The same box, checking and feedback as above.

  - end-user acceptance

  - acceptance

#### Question in the draw: l27-p-backup

A chat, with its history: "Pauline, Warehouse", Chat with the help desk.

> (Pauline, Warehouse, at the left) The file server gets a full backup on Sunday. Each night after that, it copies everything that changed since Sunday. It crashed on Thursday morning.

**Which backups does the restore need?**
(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)
- Sunday’s full and Wednesday night’s backup only (right)
- Sunday’s full and the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday backups — if chosen: That is how an incremental restore goes. These nightly backups each hold everything since Sunday, so Wednesday’s already includes the earlier days.
- Wednesday night’s backup alone, since it is the newest — if chosen: Wednesday’s holds only what changed since Sunday. Everything unchanged lives only in the full.
- Sunday’s full alone, since it is the only full one — if chosen: That brings back Sunday’s files and loses the changes from Monday to Wednesday.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: A backup of everything changed since the last full is a differential. A restore needs the last full and the latest differential, and no more.

#### Question in the draw: l27-q-diff

A chat, with its history: "Kiana, Systems", Chat with the help desk.

> (Kiana, Systems, at the left) The nightly backup has a 30-minute window and the backup disk has little space. A slow restore is fine with us, because the server rarely fails.

**Which backup kind fits?**
(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)
- Incremental: only what changed since the last backup (right)
- Full: a complete copy of everything, every single night — if chosen: A full copy every night is the slowest and biggest to make, so it breaks the window and the disk space.
- Differential: everything changed since the last full backup — if chosen: A differential grows a little every night, so it takes more time and space than an incremental.
- Synthetic full: a full built on the backup server — if chosen: A synthetic full is a complete copy, so it takes the most room on a small backup disk.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: Fastest and smallest to make is incremental. The cost is the restore, which needs the last full plus every incremental in order.

- The accepted answers shown after (Accepted answers):

After the answer: Reason: The 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies of the data, on 2 kinds of media, with 1 copy offsite. The original counts as one of the three.

- The accepted answers shown after (Accepted answers):

(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)

- In place, over the current file, to save the time of a copy — if chosen: Restoring in place overwrites the current file before anyone has compared them.
- Delete the current file first, then restore the backup in its place — if chosen: Deleting first removes the version Ramona wants to compare against.
- Run a new full backup of the drive, and compare the files later — if chosen: A new backup copies the wrong version too, and does not bring back yesterday’s file.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: A restore to an alternate location keeps the current file, which is what a comparison needs. A restore in place overwrites it.

- A synthetic full, built on the backup server from changes (right)
- A differential backup, copying changes since the last full — if chosen: A differential copies what changed since the last full. It does not build a new full copy.
- An incremental backup, copying changes since the last backup — if chosen: An incremental copies what changed since the last backup. It does not build a new full copy.
- A full backup, copying everything from the server again — if chosen: A full backup reads everything from the server again, which is the load Eda wants to avoid.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: A new full built on the backup server from the last full plus the changes is a synthetic full.

(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)
- Sunday’s full and the nightly backups from Monday to Thursday, in order (right)
- Sunday’s full and Thursday night’s backup, which holds all the changes — if chosen: That is how a differential restore goes. Thursday’s here holds only Thursday’s changes, so the other nights are needed too.
- Thursday night’s backup alone, since it is the newest one made — if chosen: Thursday’s holds only one day of changes. Everything else lives in the full and the earlier nights.

(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)
- Saturday’s full and the Sunday, Monday and Tuesday backups (right)
- Saturday’s full and only Tuesday night’s backup, the latest one — if chosen: That is how a differential restore goes. These nightly copies hold just one night of changes each.
- Tuesday night’s backup alone, since it is the newest copy made — if chosen: Tuesday’s copy holds only Tuesday’s changes.
- Saturday’s full alone, since a full backup holds everything — if chosen: The full holds the files as they were on Saturday. The changes since then are in the nightly copies.

#### Question in the draw: l27-w-evid

A chat, with its history: "Cheryl, HR", Chat with the help desk.

> (Cheryl, HR, at the left) My laptop is slow and the drive says it is almost full. Can you clean it up?

A plain table, "What you saw while checking the drive":

> Folder  |  What is in it  (the column heads)
> Downloads: a spreadsheet with about 400 rows of full credit card numbers and names
> Documents: a note that says “sell the list Friday”

**What do you do next?**
(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)
- Stop, change nothing, and tell your manager what you saw (right)
- Delete the spreadsheet and wipe the drive to protect the company — if chosen: Deleting or wiping destroys what may be evidence, and it is not your decision to make.
- Copy the spreadsheet to a USB stick to show your manager — if chosen: Copying files off the laptop changes it and starts a copy nobody has a record of. The drive is copied the proper way, by the people who handle evidence.
- Call the police yourself, right away, from your own phone — if chosen: Management is told first and decides about law enforcement. Telling the police is not the technician’s call.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: The first guess, clean it up, would have deleted evidence. Prohibited content or a crime found on a drive means: stop, leave it alone, inform management, document everything, keep the chain of custody, and let the copy be examined while the original stays unchanged.
The working:
- The ticket says “clean it up”. Test that against what you found.: The first guess is the usual one: delete big files, free space. But one folder holds 400 card numbers and a note about selling them. This is no longer a slow laptop.
- Stop and leave everything as it is.: Delete nothing, clean nothing, run no scan, do not shut it down on your own. Every change can damage evidence.
- Inform management, and write it down.: Tell your manager at once. Incident documentation: what you saw, the time, the folders, and every click you made on the laptop.
- Keep the chain of custody.: The laptop goes into a locked place, with a sheet that records who held it, when and why. Anyone who takes it signs the sheet.
- Leave the copying to the people who handle evidence.: They collect memory first, since it is lost at power-off, then make an exact copy of the drive and check it with a hash. They examine the copy, and the original stays unchanged.

- The rollback plan: the steps to undo a change that failed — if chosen: A rollback plan belongs to change management. This is an evidence ticket.
- A change freeze: a time when no changes are allowed — if chosen: A change freeze blocks changes for a period. It does not record who held a drive.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: The written record of who held the evidence, when and where is the chain of custody.

#### Question in the draw: l28-w-remote

A chat, with its history: "Eamon, Branch IT", Chat with the help desk.

A plain table, "From the desk’s notes on the Dayton branch":

> Note  (the column heads)
> The file server runs Linux with no desktop: it has only a text command line.
> Company computers outside the office must connect through the company VPN. The server has no direct line to the internet.
> Restarting a file service after hours is a standard change: no new approval is needed.

**Which tools does Eamon use, in order?**
(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)
- The VPN first, then SSH to the server (right)
- RDP straight to the server’s address — if chosen: RDP shows a Windows desktop. This server is Linux with no desktop, and it has no direct line to the internet either.
- VNC straight to the server, with nothing in front of it — if chosen: VNC shows a screen, and the server has none to show. It also has no direct line to the internet, so it could not be reached from home.
- A screen-sharing app, run by a user at the branch — if chosen: That needs a person at the branch to start it, and a server with no desktop has no screen to share.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: A Linux server with only a command line is reached with SSH, and from outside the company the way in is the VPN. RDP is for a Windows desktop and VNC would have left a door open to the internet.
The working:
- Name the favorite tool, then test it against the server.: The first guess is RDP, because it is the tool most people know. But RDP is for a Windows desktop, and note 1 says this server has no desktop. RDP is ruled out.
- Check how Eamon gets to the branch at all.: Note 2: the server is only reachable from the company network, so Eamon connects the VPN first. The VPN is not a screen tool; it is the way in.
- Pick the tool that fits a Linux server with only a command line.: SSH, Secure Shell, on port 22. The sign-in uses the technician’s own account, and the typed command restarts the file service. Note 3 makes the restart a standard change, so it needs no new approval.
- Check, then close properly.: Eamon, still at home on the VPN, opens a file from the share, and it works. The note lists the VPN, SSH, the account used and the service restarted. The VPN and SSH sessions are ended.

#### Question in the draw: l28-g-halluc

#### Question in the draw: l28-r-ai-3

A chat, with its history: "Kalinda, Desk", Chat with the help desk.

> (Kalinda, Desk, at the left) An AI tool says that error code 0x80070005 means a broken network cable. I think it is a permissions error, but the answer sounded sure.

**What do you do before telling the user?**
(the options come in an order that depends on the seed of the question)
- Check the answer against the maker’s documentation (right)
- Send it on as is, since the AI sounded certain — if chosen: Sounding sure is not accuracy. AI can state wrong things with confidence.
- Put the same question to the AI until it gives the same answer twice — if chosen: Repeating the question can repeat the same mistake.
- Paste the user’s whole ticket into the AI for a second opinion — if chosen: Pasting the ticket may send private data to a public service.

After the answer: the deciding words are marked. Reason: AI answers are checked against the maker’s documentation before anyone acts on them.

## The result

For example "40 of 40: passed" or "31 of 40: not yet", each rule above shown as met or not met, then every answer with its feedback, the missed ones first.
